newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Drunken Croats drive Moslems from Bosnian homes.
newsitem.headline: Drunken Croats drive Moslems from Bosnian homes.

text.p: Hundreds of Moslems who had returned to their pre-war homes in a Croat-controlled area of Bosnia over the last three weeks have been forced to flee again by drunken Croat mobs, officials said on Sunday.
By Sunday evening only 85 Moslems remained of the hundreds who had returned to the town of Jajce, about 100 km (60 miles) northwest of Sarajevo, and three surrounding villages.
But then even these were taken out of their village, Kruscica, by bus and were heading east towards the town of Travnik, a spokesman for the NATO-led SFOR peacekeeping force said.
"All three villages are now empty. The Moslems agreed to go. The buses were not UNHCR buses, we think they were provided by the Jajce local authorities," spokesman Adrian Wilkinson told Reuters.
Bosnian television reported that one man, Hasim Sahman, had been burned to death when his house was burned down near Jajce, and Bosnian radio said a number of Moslems' houses had been set on fire.
The Moslems said they intended to make another attempt on Tuesday to return to the villages, which were their homes before the 43-month Bosnian war.
The population of Jajce is around 98 percent Bosnian Croat, and the town is run by Croat authorities.
Wilkinson said SFOR had received a report from the United Nations International Police Task Force (IPTF) that one person had died in the village of Psenik, just south of Jajce, on Saturday night.
The report said his house was burned down. Nobody from IPTF was available to confirm the report to Reuters.
IPTF spokesman Alex Ivanko said earlier that 372 Moslems had decided over the weekend not to stay in Jajce and had moved to a police station in a nearby Moslem-controlled area.
Wilkinson said that after the last Moslems had fled Kruscica, around 250 Bosnian Croats who had gathered north and south of the village headed back to Jajce "having achieved their aim".
The office of the international community's High Representative in Bosnia said in a statement that the events were unacceptable.
It demanded that conditions be established within 48 hours "which would enable families who left Jajce to return to their homes with full guarantees for their safety".
The statement said there were indications that police might have been involved in the incidents -- a chronic problem in ethnically riven Bosnia.
British forces serving with SFOR in Bosnia were present in armoured vehicles monitoring the situation during the day.

But Wilkinson said local Bosnian Croat police were ultimately responsible for the safety of all people in the area including the returnees -- many of whom came back of their own accord and without the supervision of international organisations.
"SFOR is a military force and not a police force...The peaceful resolution of the situation in Jajce is of course the responsibility of the civil authorities," he said.
Moslems and Bosnian Croats allied with each other in 1994 under a U.S.-brokered deal and are now joined in a Moslem-Croat Federation which makes up half of post-war Bosnia.
But the federation remains divided into largely Moslem and Croat-dominated enclaves, with virtually no cooperation between the two.
Ivanko said the incidents in Jajce were "not good news".
"Jajce was one of the few areas where there was quite a substantial number of (Moslem) families who had returned to their homes over the past three weeks."

Under the Dayton peace agreement which ended the Bosnian war in November 1995, all refugees in the former Yugoslavia have the right to return to their pre-war homes. However progress has been slow throughout the region.
